title: Backup Option Prevents Multiple Saves to Symlinked Files

labels.name: bug-regression
labels.description: wrong behavior that was introduced in a previous commit (please bisect)

body:
I've done a git bisect and found that this is a regression introduced by b4d894c06709b4ae807d540dfda21ab3220a989a: the previous commit works as expected.

- Vim (version: ) behaves differently? 
I haven't checked, I don't think it's relevant for a regression like this.
- Operating system/version:
Mac OSX 10.14.5
- Terminal name/version:
iTerm2 3.2.9
- `$TERM`:
xterm-256color

### Steps to reproduce

In words:
1) Set the "backup" option on.
2) Open a symlink to a file in a different directory.
3) Write to the file. This creates a file in the backup directory.
4) Write to the file again. This one fails because it cannot overwrite the backup file created in step 3.

I wrote a script to make doing the bisect easier, it might come in handy.

```
#! /bin/bash

# Make a backup dir free of any previous files
mkdir test_backupdir

# Minimal vimrc to use that dir
printf "set backup\nset writebackup\nset backupdir=./test_backupdir\n" > test_vimrc

# Create a file and a symlink to it
touch test.txt
# Specifying the full path seems to be required: "ln -s test.txt link_to_test.txt" does not reproduce the issue
ln -s $(pwd)/test.txt link_to_test.txt

# Open the symlink and try to write to it twice
./nvim -u test_vimrc -c "w" -c "w" link_to_test.txt

# In affected versions, the second write fails with the message:
# E509: Cannot create backup file (add ! to override)
# Press ENTER or type command to continue

# Running "ls -lA test_backupdir" shows that the only file is a symlink named
# "link_to_test.txt~" pointing to the path of the test.txt file
```

### Actual behaviour

The second attempt to write to the symlink fails.

In versions with the bug, the backup file is a symlink to the real one. In versions without it, it is a real text file.

### Expected behaviour

You can write to a file (or symlink to that file) as many times as you'd like.
